title: Can Britain Feed Itself? Food security, resilience and regeneration
subtitle: A £2 insurance policy, a smarter farm system, and meaningful work
status: Draft for fact-checking. Not a government publication.

chapters.title: Can Britain feed itself?
chapters.headline: Resilient on paper, fragile in practice.
body: UK farms produce about 60% of the food the UK consumes by value, and about 72% of foods that can be grown here.
Calories are covered on paper; protein looks generous only because imported animal feed is counted in.
The fragility lies in inputs (gas-based fertiliser, imported soya), weather and the absence of any public food reserve.

chapters.title: Nature's gift
chapters.headline: World-class per hectare, land-poor per person, with soils that can recover.
body: A mild, wet Köppen Cfb climate gives a long growing season and rain-fed farming almost everywhere.
UK wheat yields are about double the world average; the world wheat-yield record was set in Lincolnshire.
Each person has about a third of the arable land a French person has, so what we grow, and who eats it, matters more than how much land we have.
Grass-clover leys at Rothamsted raised soil carbon by about a quarter in 28 years.

chapters.title: Climate is changing the odds
chapters.headline: One bad week doesn't hurt British wheat. Bad weather stacked across a season does, and that is now the pattern.
body: UK yields absorb single extremes but fail when extremes combine across one season (2020: wet autumn, dry spring, wet harvest).
Four of the five worst UK harvests on record fall in 2020-2026.
In 2026 the UK, France and Germany lost harvests together, so the neighbours trade relies on were failing too.
Warming brings new pests and diseases.

chapters.title: Hidden dependencies
chapters.headline: A loaf of bread runs on gas, diesel, ships and software.
body: The UK no longer makes its own ammonia, the starting material for nitrogen fertiliser. Food-grade CO2, a by-product of the same plants, is a recurring chokepoint.
All phosphate is imported, and less than half is used productively.
Over half of UK food is chilled or frozen, and cyber attacks have already halted supermarket supply systems.
A long power cut would break the food system faster than a bad harvest.

chapters.title: Protein, livestock and the sea
chapters.headline: Grain isn't the weak point. Imported protein feed is.
body: About half of UK wheat, barley and oats goes to animal feed, more than the global third.
Most UK feed grain could be eaten by people after mould-toxin testing, as porridge, flatbreads and biscuits if not bread.
Pigs and poultry depend on imported soya; cattle and sheep on grass use land nothing else can use.
We export the fish we catch and import the fish we eat. Mackerel and herring are an unused protein buffer.

chapters.title: Geopolitics and prices
chapters.headline: Two chokepoints in one year. Britain buys neither directly, and pays for both.
body: The Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted since February 2026; it carries LNG and up to 30% of traded fertiliser.
Black Sea grain exports have been hit since July 2026.
In a crisis, export bans spread fast and supply flows towards countries that hold stocks.
A reserve is foreign policy: no panic-buying, no hoarding, a reliable partner.

chapters.title: Food and stability
chapters.headline: It is rising prices, not empty fields, that break the peace. And people forgive scarcity sooner than unfairness.
body: 'Nine meals from anarchy' (Alfred Henry Lewis, 1906) is a slogan, not evidence. The evidence says food price levels, not volatility, are followed by unrest.
In rich countries logistics fail first: in the 2000 fuel protests Sainsbury's warned it would run out of food within days.
One household in eight is food-insecure today.
Most local resilience forums do not plan for food disruption, and Defra lacks a power to direct businesses.

chapters.title: How other countries prepare
chapters.headline: Finland, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, Germany and Japan hold food reserves. Britain has none.
body: Comparable countries hold 1-9 months of bread grain, rotate it through private firms, and fund it with small levies or defence budgets.
Switzerland drew on its protein-feed reserve in August 2026 when drought stalled river transport.
Japan shows what goes wrong: its rice reserve was run down to a third of its target and refilled too late.
The UK has no public or compulsory food stock and 'no current plans' for one.

chapters.title: The £2 insurance policy
chapters.headline: From £2 per person per year: eight weeks of complete food for everyone. Nothing wasted.
body: A complete diet can be stored: grain, pulses, oil, milk powder, canned fish, vitamins.
Old stock rotates to school meals, hospitals, food banks, millers and animal feed, so nothing is wasted. Japan already sells five-year-old reserve rice as feed.
The state can store food about ten times more cheaply than households can.
Minimal downside: a small premium, managed by buying gradually, independent audit and a legal minimum.

chapters.title: Work, wellbeing and the AI economy
chapters.headline: Meaningful work in nature: tens of thousands of good jobs, not millions. AI is the enabler, not the enemy.
body: Entry-level jobs are shrinking as AI and automation spread.
Structured time in nature measurably improves mental health, and a 1930s conservation corps improved participants' health and earnings for decades.
Farm work today is often poorly designed: seasonal, isolated and stressful.
Proposal: a regenerative transition corps working on hedges, trees, peat, AI-assisted soil monitoring, glasshouses on data-centre heat, and reserve logistics.

chapters.title: A new economy of food
chapters.headline: Price what harms, pay for what protects, and give the revenue back.
body: A carbon price arrives on imported fertiliser in 2027; carbon money is moving to durable removals such as trees, peat and biochar.
Soil-carbon offsets remain low-trust: pay for soil health directly instead.
Denmark taxes livestock emissions from 2030 and recycles the revenue into land use change.
System change fails when it is imposed on farmers and works when it pays them.

chapters.title: The plan
chapters.headline: Store. Grow for people. Fewer, better animals. Close the loops. Price the truth. Draw down carbon. Bring people with us.
body: Store: a rotating national reserve from £2 per person per year, plus seed, nitrogen and oils.
Grow for people: less feed grain; more pulses, vegetables and fruit; glasshouses on waste heat.
Fewer, better animals: pigs and poultry sized to UK protein supply; cattle and sheep on grass.
Close the loops: phosphorus recovery from sewage; licensed heat-treated food waste for pigs (Japan/Korea model).
Price the truth: carbon tax on imported fertiliser, a livestock levy, revenue recycled to farmers and households.
Draw down carbon: hedges and trees on poor land, peat rewetting where it makes sense, verified rock-dust trials.
People: a regenerative transition corps, local food plans, fair rationing rules, a legal power to direct.

known_corrections_to_earlier_briefings: Food inflation 'could reach 9% this year' is overtaken: 1.3% in Aug 2026.
Gemini claims of +300% farm labour, precision-fermentation patriotism, vertical farms as grid stabilisers, a global carbon market by 2030, and 'UK ranks with Ukraine's chernozem' are unsupported.
The Lagi '210' riot threshold doesn't apply to the rebased FAO index.
